item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
Responses:

+ show block
– hide block

I presume that you and the staff team can delete such responses and leave a verbal warning, which I'm fine about since these posts won't be about the bad reviews but the spamming its self.

Staff only delete posts that contain severe rulebreaking, to keep users accountable for what they post. Doing that also allows for greater transparency—just because staff know that a post was deleted doesn't mean that site members in general know that a post was removed.

Furthermore, users often create multiple "replacement" posts or threads when they think something they posted is missing. Dropping a staff warning doesn't always guarantee that spamming will stop, or that the spammer will notice the staff warnings to begin with.

This was a new response, on the help critique forums that if you scrolled 3 to 2 pages you'll probably find, so I simply assumed that this was still done.

Can you provide a direct link to the post? The forum threads shift fairly often day-to-day, so what you've seen on page 2-3 will definitely be different from what I'm seeing 19 hours later. If I know the staff member who's using an outdated placeholder, they can be updated much faster.

Plus for none staff reviewers, they do rely on 'no response threads' and newer works to critique.

Is this something that you can confirm with examples and comparisons? I've tended to see a more or less even split between newer reviewers responding to threads with no replies versus threads that already have replies. Again though, it might depend on the time of day that the forums are viewed.

It's that hypocritical mindset that makes me believe with this statement. Notifying reviewers that their response didn't help the author in a sufficient way

Newer placeholders should ideally implement the following link: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-9804362/so-you-want-to-be-a-concept-reviewer

Ideally, staff addressing problematic feedback should be encouraging the reviewer in question to improve their critique themselves, rather than expecting staff to essentially write one for them.

while replying with a message that doesn't help the author in any sufficient way, feels very one-sided.

Are you stating that you feel that noting feedback is problematic does not help the author?

Even though the staff are doing the same thing as the bad reviewers, they're in the right?

Staff are inherently not "doing the same thing as the bad reviewers", as they are present in the thread not to post a review, but to address breach of forum rules/etiquette. A reviewer who posts a low-quality review is not present in the thread to address any sort of forum guideline in the same capacity.

I think the disconnect here is the belief that if anyone posts in a review thread, for whatever reason, they're obligated to give a review. Is this correct?

ETA: also, as a general note, there's no need to sign your posts. Everyone can already see your username at the top of every comment you post, and this is a forum discussion, not an email chain. It seems a little silly to re-introduce yourself repeatedly when again, the associated username is fairly obvious.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
Hey Zyn, sorry for the last post it was… unprofessional,

Next time I will use the 'new post'. (I did wonder why the front page post was so far back.)

+ Response
- Response

what should be done to prevent authors from taking advantage of that and "helping" people get more reviews by spamposting low quality material on other threads?

You're definitely right there, there's not really another way of replying to many short spam threads other than using short warnings, but I presume that you and the staff team can delete such responses and leave a verbal warning, which I'm fine about since these posts won't be about the bad reviews but the spamming its self.

The forum guidelines have changed, and reviews are no longer automatically given/prioritized to threads that have fewer replies. Rather, authors are asked to contact reviewers directly to request feedback.

I knew that from the start, although you still do both, take my example from before:
"This feedback is vague and unhelpful. As per the site's Criticism Policy, forum critique should be relatively in-depth. Staff prioritize threads with no response, and by offering poor critique, you may be preventing an author from receiving the critique they are seeking."

This was a new response, on the help critique forums that if you scrolled 3 to 2 pages you'll probably find, so I simply assumed that this was still done. Plus for none staff reviewers, they do rely on 'no response threads' and newer works to critique.

This admittedly comes off as rather accusatory. If you feel that staff template responses sound like half-arsed complaining that targets users personally while making it seem like staff are self-congratulating, please provide examples of alternate wording that can be used for said templates.

Apologies for this, like I said "Unprofessional." However my statement came out wrong, it's not that staff are blatantly screaming out of their lungs "I am good! your response is bad!" It's that hypocritical mindset that makes me believe with this statement. Notifying reviewers that their response didn't help the author in a sufficient way while replying with a message that doesn't help the author in any sufficient way, feels very one-sided. Even though the staff are doing the same thing as the bad reviewers, they're in the right?

All in all, I can already tell you won't budge and won't do anything about it. It's was only a minor critique anyway, sorry for wasting your time.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
As a general note, for this thread, please use the "new post" button at the bottom left of the screen—that way the comment will nest properly with the other newer comments. Typically when checking this thread, staff don't look at the first posts (which, if comments are posted correctly, are the oldest queries).

+ show block
– hide block

I understand that the person who gave the obscure review in the first place is definitely incorrect, but I would argue that the staff (let's just say staff for simplicity) is equally in the wrong, causing the exact problems the other reviewer is causing:

Giving absolutely no response at all

What do you recommend that staff do instead to address problematic critique?

Also, if staff/reviewers should be obligated to provide a critique if they're going to comment on someone providing low-quality critique, what should be done to prevent authors from taking advantage of that and "helping" people get more reviews by spamposting low quality material on other threads?

Adding to the amount of response, lessening the chance of writer getting responded to, even more than the different reviewer

The forum guidelines have changed, and reviews are no longer automatically given/prioritized to threads that have fewer replies. Rather, authors are asked to contact reviewers directly to request feedback.

Sure, I'm fine if you complain to a vague response and add your reviews and opinions as well, but if you just leave a half-arse "I am good! your response is bad!" and no review (sorry for my bashful language),

This admittedly comes off as rather accusatory. If you feel that staff template responses sound like half-arsed complaining that targets users personally while making it seem like staff are self-congratulating, please provide examples of alternate wording that can be used for said templates.

then that is disappointing to the writer who is actually waiting for a response and a review,

Again, authors should reach out to reviewers to request feedback rather than just waiting without reaching out at all. We have a thread for this: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-13282692/how-to-get-more-reviews

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
Hey, I'm not sure whether anyone will respond to this since the last post was 2 years ago! But I'll ask anyway.

This probably sounds pretty petty, and an easily changeable complaint but it happens quite often and it's so bothersome. It's really annoying (for me personally) when, not just staff, but any viewer who replies to a vague, incomplete review to a writer on the help idea critique, with

this feedback is vague and unhelpful. As per the site's Criticism Policy, forum critique should be relatively in-depth. Staff prioritize threads with no response, and by offering poor critique, you may be preventing an author from receiving the critique they are seeking.

I understand that the person who gave the obscure review in the first place is definitely incorrect, but I would argue that the staff (let's just say staff for simplicity) is equally in the wrong, causing the exact problems the other reviewer is causing:

  • Giving absolutely no response at all

&

  • Adding to the amount of response, lessening the chance of writer getting responded to, even more than the different reviewer

This hypocritical mindset is why I'm so irritated.

I believe if a member 'staff' doesn't have any review or input to give, then they should not reply at all. Sure, I'm fine if you complain to a vague response and add your reviews and opinions as well, but if you just leave a half-arse "I am good! your response is bad!" and no review (sorry for my bashful language), then that is disappointing to the writer who is actually waiting for a response and a review, buts accompanies a tv drama instead.

I'm sorry if I was extremely forward. But this was bothering me for a while and I feel this could have been an apparent fix.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
ETA: okay, here we go. Will try to make this brief. Aside from the background post already noted by McB, here's my replies

To ihp:

+ show block
– hide block

But the new, required format for pitching ideas is a baffling and bizarre idea that will just serve to scare off new authors and irritate veterans.

I don't see much of the former happening (we had almost 60 new threads posted today alone, plenty following the new format and a few authors have actually stated that they are happy for it since it helps outline the conceptualization process better) and the latter can be easily dealt with if necessary; say, if someone links their author page then they can post an ideas thread without needing the template. The new process is still being tweaked to see how much it helps both reviewers and authors.

do we really have to specify what our page layout is? […] And the "genre" portion

Both have been edited to be optional.

What if the format is hard to explain succinctly, or if it has an interactive component in some way?

The author can just put "there will be an interactive component". I'm not sure how a format would be difficult to explain succinctly—do you have examples?

There's a difference between having standards of quality and gatekeeping, and this is dangerously close to the latter.

If you have suggestions for alternatives that are less gatekeep-y and will ensure that authors can receive solid reviews and reviewers aren't getting burned out, please state them.

To ModernMajorGeneral:

+ show block
– hide block

Agreed - I don't have a problem with a pro forma layout for idea pitches but this is badly done. What even is "emotional" as a genre? No "fantasy" or "science fiction" options?

That section has been made optional. What is your suggestion for a better list of examples that can be used in the template?

Saying "these are just examples and you can put whatever genre you want in" might be true but it's dangerous to assume that giving examples like this, in a rule post that for many new posters will be one of the only things they might read on the forum, will not influence expectations of what people think is supposed to be on the site.

Incidentally, part of the reason that section exists is to indicate to new authors that horror isn't the only thing on the SCP wiki.

I think the central narrative section is redundant if you have an elevator pitch section (I mean, if your elevator pitch is good, you don't need any of the other sections to start a productive discussion about an idea, and if it's bad, why make them mandatory?). Page layout and even a hook/attention-grabber are not always things I consider to be particularly important in constructing an idea initially.

For the most part, the new template is not really for well-established authors for whom writing an elevator pitch comes easily. For new authors who don't have the experience of seeing a successful article come to fruition from conceptualization, many of them may not realize that narratives even exist, or have the perspective that they are writing alongside thousands of other articles and what they have might have already been done before.

As stated to ihp, if you as an experienced author feel like the template restricts your ability to seek conceptual critique, it's not difficult to add in a "if you have an author page, you can waive the need for a template" caveat.

Even something simple like page type is not necessarily useful […] but forcing them to make a decision right at the start of the page is unnecessarily restrictive to the writing process.

I don't see where anyone is forced to stick to a certain format—that section exists because sometimes reviewers have actually had to ask "are you writing an SCP article or a tale".

the number of people posting ideas vastly outweighs the number of people willing to respond to them

This is the case, and it has been a problem for years.

and the staff have no other response than to throw up increasingly onerous obstacles in the way.

The purpose of the template isn't to provide an obstacle, it's to hopefully make the reviewing process smoother for both authors and reviewers. One of the biggest concerns in the Ideas Critique forum is that reviewers are burning themselves out.

Whether it's reading material they didn't like/had to basically drag the author through the process of making something workable, or just spending a lot of time writing high-effort critique on material that was quickly discarded or simply didn't have the same amount of effort put in, it's not sustainable with the current growth of authors and comparatively very very very small pool of new reviewers.

Of course, we're always open to hearing alternatives. But without more reviewers helping out, there's not much that can be done to address the overflow problem except nudge authors to be more conscientious with what they're asking reviewers to invest time in. When the other solutions brought up included "just ignore the threads that clearly won't stand a chance on the mainsite" or "lock the forums entirely a few times a week", this step seemed like the least extreme.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
Agreed - I don't have a problem with a pro forma layout for idea pitches but this is badly done. What even is "emotional" as a genre? No "fantasy" or "science fiction" options? Saying "these are just examples and you can put whatever genre you want in" might be true but it's dangerous to assume that giving examples like this, in a rule post that for many new posters will be one of the only things they might read on the forum, will not influence expectations of what people think is supposed to be on the site.

I think the central narrative section is redundant if you have an elevator pitch section (I mean, if your elevator pitch is good, you don't need any of the other sections to start a productive discussion about an idea, and if it's bad, why make them mandatory?). Page layout and even a hook/attention-grabber are not always things I consider to be particularly important in constructing an idea initially.

Even something simple like page type is not necessarily useful - how many ideas receive advice about how they would be better as a tale or a regular SCP or a joke SCP? Again you could argue that it is helpful to get newbies to at least think about these things, but forcing them to make a decision right at the start of the page is unnecessarily restrictive to the writing process.

With the charge of staff taking no fun allowed attitudes, my alternative impression (which may or may not be more charitable, and may or may not be correct) is that the number of people posting ideas vastly outweighs the number of people willing to respond to them and the staff have no other response than to throw up increasingly onerous obstacles in the way. I don't offer any other solutions to this myself, but at least responding directly to this (with limiting authors posting new threads and such, which I see has now been implemented and is probably a good idea) is more palatable than interfering with the creative process directly.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
I genuinely despise what's happening with regards to how we handle ideas critique and submitting drafts on the forums. Not having drafts in the ideas forums, sure. Needing greenlights keeps dreck out of the draft's forums. But the new, required format for pitching ideas is a baffling and bizarre idea that will just serve to scare off new authors and irritate veterans. Standardized formatting would be appreciated, but large parts of this are redundant or poorly constructed— do we really have to specify what our page layout is? What if the format is hard to explain succinctly, or if it has an interactive component in some way? And the "genre" portion makes me gag:

Genre: Horror, Drama/Emotional, Comedy, Action, History, Other (specify)

I realize that the "Other" portion means that "Just say what genre you want", but to me, it reads like "check this box if it doesn't fit into any of the above arbitrarily chosen categories".

This is a bureaucratic form that I'd expect to find in-universe on the desk of a pencil pusher a Site-19, not on a forum for a weird fiction writing website where people are meant to flex their creative muscles to see if their ideas are workable or not. Hell, I've had inspiration for the ideas I'm writing about as I make the forum post for these ideas, and this just restricts them.

I recently talked with a member of the site who's become largely inactive in recent years, and they got the impression that the Staff had gotten an attitude of "No Fun Allowed" recently. I didn't see it at first, but now, I really, really do. There's a difference between having standards of quality and gatekeeping, and this is dangerously close to the latter.

item.title: Re: Complaints Thread
item.content:encoded:
I realize I might be stepping on some toes here, which isn't my intention whatsoever. My reason for bringing this up is it appears the mods might've jumped the gun on one of the disciplinary cases resulting in a potentially unjust ban of a user.

The case I am bring up can be found here: http://05command.wikidot.com/forum/t-12451853/disciplinary-burning-fist

The infraction was classified as malicious down voting; however, the user had only made 17 votes overall. According to the linked post the individual had made 1 up vote and 16 down votes, 4 of which were on pages with pride themes. While I am unsure if this individual had received a ban or not the amount of votes is very small, and the reaction in my eyes seems a tad extreme for a perma ban to even be considered.

This individual could be hard to impress, only leaving up votes on articles that are "really good" or many other reasons. As for the pride themes I think it is definitely within the realm of possibility this was coincidence; the pool is just too small to accurately gauge malicious intent. Depending how widely used those page themes are this individual was essentially walking through a mine field with a blind fold on. I do not know how much weight a small number of down votes on pages with pride themes hold; however, if 4 down votes is enough to potentially land a perma the weighing may need to be reworked.

In comparison with the first post I linked there was another user whom down voted 111 articles for using "ACS" and received a six month ban. That is malicious down voting beyond the shadow of a doubt. Although in the first post I mentioned the I do not believe there was enough of a case to build up that could warrant any interference.
Article of reference: http://05command.wikidot.com/forum/t-12664206/disciplinary-styrius

My concern is not only with the lack of a case being built up, but also the possibility the user could've been banned due to their personal tastes violating one of the first protections listed on the site under the list of actions that will not result in a ban "Voting on any article based solely on your own opinion of its quality or merits." If this kind of reaction became a trend it could potentially strike enough fear resulting in users not voting out of fear of the ban hammer, effectively killing the quality control system.

I don't doubt the mod team had only the best intentions in mind; with joining the site being as easy as it is understandable that quick actions are sometimes necessary to avoid incidents. Obviously I'm no mod so maybe I'm missing something or misinterpreted the situation, but just in case I thought I'd put my two cents in. Having been a long time lurker who recently joined I only want to see the site continue to do well. Sorry for how long winded this is.

item.title: Re: Complaints ... in general
item.content:encoded:
Hi. Forum Criticism and Site Criticism Operational Staff here.

+ show block
– hide block

First, this site is supposed to be a fun way to contribute to the ongoing canon and story of the SCP Foundation.

Well, sort of. The site is meant to be a fun thing to contribute to, but there isn't a canon or ongoing story. If there was, we'd be dancing an impossible dance of keeping track of what every article has to make sure it is canonically sound. That's a lot of reading, and not everyone has that much time.

More accurately, the site is meant to contribute stories to entertain an audience. Some of those stories are contained, others take bits and pieces of other stories. Nothing is set in stone, otherwise if someone just up and left there'd be a big hole where their articles used to be and a lot of things without context.

When I first joined, you wrote an actual proposal, people looked it over, and approved it or not.

Yep. We still do that. Only difference is that the Forum Criticism Team isn't overloaded with poorly written drafts. We have the greenlight system now to maintain that a little bit. There's still approval, but it's for each step of the creation process.

I've literally seen near spot on copies of other SCPs waiting for approval that had reviews telling them they weren't written like real SCPs. I've seen reviewers comment on SCP proposals that were the dumbest things I've ever seen, and they've been approved. You people need to get consistency here.

Everyone is different. In the end, this is a site that contributes writing to entertain an audience, and reviewers are kind of like beta testers in that regard. Everyone likes different things. There's no being consistent in that.

NOW, you have to have the very idea given a green light by TWO writing snobs who clearly don't have any idea how your own source materials work.

The requirements for people to give greenlights are:

  • Being on the Butterfly Squad Roster, which are dedicated and trusted reviewers.
  • Meeting the criteria for an Author Page, which is having three successful articles.
  • Having selected an article for the Reviewers' Spotlight, an opportunity given to those that have demonstrated clear, constructive, and fantastic quality in their reviews
  • And being staff, which is consists of people that have a dedication to the site policies and, in terms of the crit teams, a finder to the pulse of what works on the site.

"Writing snobs" might be one way to say it, but understand that using that is the exact wrong way to get people to be willing to review your work.

Yet you approve those and bypass other good ideas I've seen here because you're being gatekeepers instead of being actual keepers of lore.

Not everything that gets posted to the site gets approved. Some people just post without getting a look from other people. Those usually hit the deletion threshold and are removed in the site within a day or two. If you are referring to stuff from Series 1, that was 10 years ago. Our standards have changed dramatically since then. You'll see a lot less of the issues you've pointed out in stuff from Series 4 and 5.

You've put up too many walls to exclude people, and it's making the newer SCPs weaker and making the lore come apart from the source.

Again, no lore is necessary to write for the site. Furthermore, our quality control has actually allowed for very strong works. See SCP-4281, SCP-4504, and SCP-4236, all articles that went through the new processes.

I hope you fix it. But you probably won't.

Of course not, because there's nothing to fix. Our crit teams aren't being overworked for the exact zero pay they are given, the site's quality of work continues to grow. A few users may be upset that their concept doesn't get approved, but there isn't anything stopping them from taking the crit and reworking their idea, nor is there any obligation to write for the site.

Alternatively, if you'd like to bypass the greenlight policy, you may bring your draft to the critique IRC Chatroom, #thecritters. However, I ask that you please be polite, as we are unpaid volunteers and do not take kindly to rude behavior or vehement demands.

item.title: Complaints ... in general
item.content:encoded:
I'm sure everyone who reads this is going to comment that I'm just having sour grapes, or that I'm bitter about not being accepted. That's the easier way to dismiss this complaint and so it will be, but I'm making it anyway so maybe a few more people will speak up.

First, this site is supposed to be a fun way to contribute to the ongoing canon and story of the SCP Foundation. I completely understand wanting to keep things similar and universally conitinual. That does NOT mean being the gatekeepers and blocking the way for people to contribute things. By this I mean the rules for contribution.

When I first joined, you wrote an actual proposal, people looked it over, and approved it or not. The problem then was writing snobs who don't even know the sources they're looking at. I've literally seen near spot on copies of other SCPs waiting for approval that had reviews telling them they weren't written like real SCPs. I've seen reviewers comment on SCP proposals that were the dumbest things I've ever seen, and they've been approved. You people need to get consistency here.

NOW, you have to have the very idea given a green light by TWO writing snobs who clearly don't have any idea how your own source materials work. Have you guys even read some of these SCPs? I love to listen to them being read and acted out by "Dr. Miller" on YouTube, better known as the Volgun. Have you heard the few of them he's made commentary on that you guys actually approved?? Too many redactions, stupid or canonically incorrect containment procedures, or just plain terrible ideas? Yet you approve those and bypass other good ideas I've seen here because you're being gatekeepers instead of being actual keepers of lore. You've put up too many walls to exclude people, and it's making the newer SCPs weaker and making the lore come apart from the source.

I don't care if you think I'm just bitter, but I'm not speaking up just for my own writings, but others I've read on here. I hope you fix it. But you probably won't.
